His cable tester hung like an award no one had bothered to polish. He rocked on the balls of his work boots, shoulder already pointed at the employee lot.

“So what’s the protocol for testing these lockers against actual rainfall?” Tess asked. “The manual mentions a spray bar, but I don’t see one installed.”

“Manuals always run ahead of the hardware.” He lifted only his eyes. “You’ll want to talk to Maintenance Scheduling; I just terminate the lines and tag the ports.”

She shifted, heel grinding a snail of water off the concrete. “Maintenance keeps bouncing me to ‘Hardware Readiness,’ and that inbox just autoresponds with ticket numbers. What’s the real test sequence?”

He wiped rain off the tester’s rubber bumper, looked through her like a bad preview. “Can’t give you one. My sheet says Graphical Target Verify and Walk Away. Anything else lands on another shift.”

“There is no other shift. Yesterday’s rain got inside locker seven and soaked Pynchon. Do you wait for a storm or simulate?”

He shrugged, the zip-tie ferns on his radio antenna shivering. “Look, the spec is thirty minutes at fifteen psi through a calibrated nozzle. Hydraulics keeps those nozzles in a cage across campus. Use the requisition form.”

Tess said, teeth sanding the words to knife-strips, “Do NOT get Facilities Hydraulics involved. Last time they invoiced Library Acquisitions sixteen hundred dollars for a single hose. Just tell me the set-up you’d run if you had to do it yourself today.”

The HEPA vents exhaled, a soft mechanical sigh that made the polyethylene tubing tremble like nervous spaghetti. Ilya’s chip sat clamped under the stereoscope, its channels glittering with trapped sapphires of air. The wall clock read 3:11. He had thirty-four minutes before the bench lights would snap off like a judge’s gavel.

“Camila, I’ve got a microfluidic maze full of bubbles—what’s the quickest way to purge them without popping the antibodies?”

She didn’t look up from the tip box. “Have you tried the degassing rig up front? It’s on the west bench; just clamp and let vacuum do the rest.”

He swallowed the urge to point out he’d already tried that—twice—and instead kept his voice level. “Vacuum alone won’t cut it; the bubbles are trapped in a 40 µm ridge. Do you crank up the back-pressure or run sonication?”

Camila slid another tip into its foam cradle. The soft click sounded like a timer. “Honestly, I just hand it off to whoever’s on instrument duty—sorry, I’ve got a meeting in ten and I’m still counting tips.”

There it was: the polite brick wall. Ilya felt sweat bead under his bouffant cap. His antibodies had survived three weeks of bench work; they weren’t going to die to a bubble posse. “Do NOT sonicate this—my probe’s already cooked a chip this month. So, back-pressure pulse or something else?”

The nurse sharks drifted above like bored commuters on a subway in slow-motion. Layla locked her elbows against the gift-shop counter, phone in one fist, receipt in the other folding itself into origami stress. Two rows of shark plushies watched, black button eyes promising no wisdom.

"Look," she said, leaning a fraction closer, "spell it out for me: do I pee on the stick first or tell Mateo I'm late and let him panic with me?"

Ignatius flipped a T-shirt so the tag tucked under. His wrist flicked like someone swatting a fly he’d already given up on. "Depends how you like your anxiety portions. I get off shift in five, so whichever’s faster?"

Air smelled of burnt espresso drifting up from the kiosk, overlaying the salt. Somewhere behind them, a child squealed at the same note as the aquarium’s emergency exit alarm. Layla’s jaw ticked. "Don't flip the whole damn thing into some dramatic announcement, that's off the table. Just—straight answer, Ignatius."

Tuesday night, the old depot smelled of burnt popcorn and wet concrete. Fluorescent tubes flickered above the grid of repair-shop photos, thirty laminated rectangles curling at their taped corners. Pavel Zielinski stood beneath them juggling two battered Nikons and a dented thermos. Deadline dawned in eighteen hours and he lacked an ending frame.

He spotted the only other soul: a woman in high-vis orange reading the ingredient list on a protein bar as if it might bite. Staff badge, clipboard, the universal uniform of reluctant authority. Pavel stepped closer, boots crunching on epoxy grit. “Could you pick one shot from the row on the end that feels like ‘done’? I only need the photo number—ten seconds, promise.”

She didn’t look up. “Um—look at number fifteen? It’s the one with the wrench.”

“I shot that one. Need a fresh closing image.”

“Gotcha.” She tapped the clipboard with her thumbnail, tempo of a ticking meter. “Maybe talk to one of the artists upstairs.”

“They’ve all ghosted.” Pavel pointed at the remaining lineup. “So, from the remaining eighteen, which gives you that ‘this story’s over’ click?”

A bus exhaled beyond the archway. The woman finally raised her eyes. “The coffee-pot repair one feels like a wrap to me.”

He winced. “Don’t use the coffee-pot frame. It’s overexposed.”

ion travelling down through the stone and into the cast-iron grate where Flavia knelt. One gloved hand steadied the boxed strain gauge, the other gripped a clipboard that had only three lines of pencil left unfilled. She needed one clean fact before she climbed back to street-level.  

“Look, all I need is the short version—will a 50 mm gauge survive winter cycling on lime mortar?”  

Mujtaba’s helmet dangled from two fingers like a bell without a tongue. “Ask the manufacturer; I just tag the cracks for photos.” His eyes kept flicking to the stone stairs, the quickest way back to the car before the frozen peas became a single soggy lump.  

Flavia’s pen tapped the page. “Their tech sheet’s vague. You’ve installed dozens of these—does the wire fatigue?”  

“I leave the wiring to the graduate students. Could you check with them instead?”  

“I am the graduate student.” The pen stopped tapping. “Field data’s due Monday. Does drift scale with temperature range?”  

Flavia thought it a reasonable question; Mujtaba’s sigh suggested otherwise. “Drift scales with everything. Talk to maintenance; I’m late for another call-out.”  

A rumble of traffic—diesel, wet limestone, and something that smelled alarmingly like burnt toast drifted over the canal. Flavia recited the next obstacle like a spell to keep him anchored: “They redirected me here. If we epoxy the blocks, do NOT use the rapid-cure version—bond failure last time nearly snapped the gauge. What’s your safe temp threshold?”

Friday, two weeks before Mid-Autumn, and the table was already sticking to Kiran’s elbows. Steam from the tofu stall drifted over like a drunk friend, clinging. Under the turquoise LED glow he pinched a flyer off the receipt spike—FairWork 2023—and slid it under a paper cup like bait.  

“Hey,” he said, “can I ask you something quick before the dinner rush implodes?”  

Vesna’s coat hung off one shoulder; the other was aimed at the taxis glowing by the curb. A ride-share icon pulsed silent on her phone. “If it’s short—I’ve got a driver circling.”  

Kiran tapped the flyer. “Remember you quit your dad’s shop? How’d you stop feeling like you were leaving him to rot?”  

“Went to the ASSOC, talked to Wong. File a formal family-labor transfer request, then walk. You can look him up; his cubicle’s still near the restrooms.”  

“I already did the paperwork. Still feels like I’m choosing my PhD over their retirement eggs.” Kiran leaned closer, blocking the motion of the next customer without seeming to. “So let me be blunt—do NOT tell me to stay weekends and ease out gradual. That option is off the table; it just strings them along.”

Greer’s boot still dripped, each tap on the flagstone counting down the minutes until tomorrow’s forum. She’d rehearsed a dozen versions of *I got us lost on Miners’ Spur* and every one tasted like wet wool.  

“I screwed the navigation on Miners’ Spur and I need exactly one sentence to tell the club so they’ll still let me post routes next month.”  

Behind the counter Eoghan rubbed at a scratched flashlight, eyes cutting to the clock. “You could send them the incident form and let the mountain write the apology for you, but I’m about to clock out.”  

She pressed on. “The form just lists checkpoints and I need something human. Like: ‘I re-plot after every cloud bank’ or whatever feels honest but punchy.”  

He clipped his carabiner of keys to his belt. “Try the club Facebook, they love concise groveling. My ride’s idling.”  

Greer smelled the dusk turning colder and felt her patience shrink. “Do NOT use the Facebook group—they’re roasters there. Do NOT name the route publicly or the local sheep farmers will tear into me if they find tracks on their land. Just a concise explanation that owning the mistake without attracting vultures.”

Aminael thumped his elbow onto the laminated counter, right next to the duck-sauce caddy, and blurted the question he’d rehearsed for three nights. “How do you forgive your brother when he still hasn’t paid you back three grand?”

Katja’s sponge stopped dead on a chipped bowl. Eleven minutes until the bus, and now philosophy hour. “Maybe try r/relationships. Crowdsourcing fixes everything now.”

“I’m serious. He’s family; I want boundaries that don’t start a civil war. Ideas?”

She slid the bowl onto a drying towel, already tasting freedom at the far end of the block. “Write the debt off, write the guy off, or hire a mediator—anything outside my shift.”

A warning flare rose in Aminael’s throat. “Whatever you do, don’t tell me to ‘just forget the money.’ That’s off the table. I’m broke, not stupid.”

Celine stepped into the tungsten puddle, cable tails snagging her sneakers. Neon buzzed overhead like wasps above a spilled soda. She tapped a rhythm on the notebook margin—sync, sync, sync.

“Hey, quick one—how do I keep three rings of CV in sync without the clock drifting?”

Rohan shifted the backpack higher; one strap was already through the door. Lukewarm beer sloshed against the inside of the bottle as he lifted it. “Ask Sam, not me. He’s running patching workshops Tuesdays.”

“Sam bailed. Need a patch that won’t drift over forty-five minutes. Any clever trick?” Her pen hovered—she could not write “canceled.” Writing was acknowledging.

“Grab a Kompakt module, lock everything to its internal crystal. Works fine.” Rohan’s thumb flicked the phone awake: ramen emoji incoming.

Celine’s shoulders stiffened. Memories of thirty frozen faces listening to stuttering sine waves pinged behind her eyes. “Do NOT run this off a laptop. I lost an entire set to buffer dropouts once.”

Ridwan’s reflection floated in the dark monitor glass: hair flat from the bike helmet, eyes pink from spreadsheets. Beneath the hum of LEDs he heard the data logger tick—sixty, tick, ninety, tick—like a cheap metronome.

“These humidity spikes started two nights ago—any idea what usually causes that kind of yo-yo?”

Isadora’s keys clinked against the gate. “You’ll want facilities; their name’s on the contact sheet by the elevator.” She slid one arm into her coat, angling toward the elevator herself.

“They already swapped the sensor and the port. Same glitch on brand-new hardware.”

“Then try IT. Logger software updates, could be a driver thing.”

Ridwan scrolled; the graph jittered like a lie-detector. “Drivers didn’t change; logs prove that. What else trips a forty-point swing?”

Check sheets, boxes, exit—Isadora’s mental checklist. “Check the loading-dock doors maybe; big air blast would do it.”

“Docks were closed both nights—guard signed off. Something local in here.”

“I’ve got a ferry. Ask the shift supervisor; he’ll follow up tomorrow.” She thumbed her phone: 4:48.

Ridwan felt the report deadline hiss behind his ears. “Look, whatever you suggest, do NOT tell me to phone the vendor hotline again—those people read scripts and waste my evenings.”

Giselle stepped over a coil of chicken wire, clutching her folder like a life raft. “Hey, sorry to interrupt — I just need to waterproof this fish head by Friday.”

Harlan didn’t look up from the menu. A bead of coffee clung to the mug’s chipped rim. “Friday's cutting it close, but good luck.”

“Right, but you built it. What would you do about light drizzle on parade day?”

“Honestly, I'd reschedule. Parade routes aren’t waterproof.”

She closed the folder with a soft smack. “Rescheduling is off the table. Thought about marine varnish?”

“Varnish stinks up everything for days. You want the workshop reeking?” he asked, gaze still on the laminate page.

“It’s only the head. Outside. Plenty of airflow.”

“Unless the forecast turns and it's blowing straight back through the bay. Not my circus.”

Giselle felt the drip hit her scarf again; cold, steady. “Focus, please. If varnish is out, what's Plan B?”

Harlan folded the menu and stuck it in his back pocket. “Ask maintenance, they're paid to care about fish heads.”

“Maintenance redirected me to you.”

“Classic pass-the-knot. Look, I've got burrito places to be.”

She planted herself between him and the doorway. “Do NOT use silicone sealers. Tried it on a dolphin last year, peeled like a bad sunburn.”

The motion puck over the returns desk kept flicking on, off, on again, as though it couldn’t decide whether either human was worth the wattage. Genevieve stepped around its cone of light and shook the rain off her note. “Listen, I just need to make one corner bright enough to read by—no rewiring, I’m renting. What’s the brightest clamp lamp you’ve got?”

Pascal balanced the box of LED strips against his hip with the practiced slump of someone twenty minutes from freedom. “Brightest clamp’s the sixty-watt equivalent LED over on aisle seven, but you could honestly grab one anywhere. We’re closing soon.”

She’d already lost one desk to a clamp bulb’s slow bake. Genevieve cut him off before he could point. “Whatever you do, don’t point me at clamp bulbs; I’ve already melted one desk. They run hot. What about plug-in pendants?”

The cracked glass made prison-bar shadows on the counter when Ione slapped her palm down. “Hey, sorry to snag you—your manager said you had the editable PDF. I need to lay out the art-walk map, and I can’t get the layering right on my laptop.”

Gopal’s thumb drummed the courier-bag buckle like a metronome overdue. The alley duty clock in his head ticked louder than the fan. “Yeah, thumb drive’s in the bag. Should be all tagged and ready.”

Ione’s fingers already flapped for it. “Great. Are there street-grid templates or do I have to freehand everything?”

“Templates folder’s on there. If it looks messy—” his shoulders lifted, tectonic but polite— “just ditch the layers and start over; nobody’s judging.”

“Starting over triples the print cost.” She scrolled imaginary numbers on the curling map. “Is there an unlocked InDesign file? Something vector?”

“Any vector in the pack will open in Inkscape,” Gopal said, edging half a step toward the doorframe. “Look under ‘source-mats.’ Close enough.”

She shook her head so hard the oldest Sharpie rolled. “Tried Inkscape already—keeps converting fonts to outlines. I’m on a Mac, need something lightweight that won’t corrupt. Do NOT give me anything that boots through Sketch; it crashed my last file.”

Ronit stood by the folding table, one earbud in, the other dangling like it had given up. His sneakers were clay-spattered, his hands in his hoodie pocket. Parisa assumed he was the tech. She’d been told someone would be here.

“What’s the quickest way to tune these bells up a whole tone without cracking them?” she asked.

He didn’t look up. “Fire 'em again.”

“They’re already glaze-fired to 04. I meant an after-firing tweak—sanding, filing?”

He scratched his wrist. “Talk to Marquez.”

She tried again. “Professor Marquez delegated this to volunteers. The path opens Sunday.”

“Then fire them again.”

Parisa’s fingers tapped the spine of her field notebook, still clipped shut. “The schedule doesn’t allow another bisque. How about sanding inside the lip?”

“You’ll dull the glaze. Look—I’ve gotta pack orders before five.”

She stepped closer, eyes on the row of bells between them and the window. “I only need the ones between here and the window. Two dozen. What’s the safest grit?”

“No idea. Ask downstairs.”

She exhaled slowly. “Do NOT tell me to use a belt sander—my last two bells exploded on contact. Sandpaper?”

Ronit finally looked at her. Not helpfully. Just... looking.

Colm stood in navy scrubs two sizes too big, coat half-on, already halfway to the rear exit. His eyes flicked to the wall clock every ten seconds. Today he was covering for Lam, who’d called in with a sick kid, and he was supposed to clock out at three-thirty. His car sat in the loading zone with the hazards on, a coffee turning cold in the cup-holder.

“Hi—sorry, are you the tech who signs off on oxygen concentrator maintenance?” Shirin called out.

Colm stopped, one arm in his sleeve. “Depends whose signature you need. Mine’s no good unless you’ve got a work order.”

“All I need is the preventive-maintenance schedule. One of the units wheezes at night and the user’s on a research protocol.”

“Forms are in the supply closet. Lam handles schedules; he’s out today.”

Shirin’s jaw tightened. “Lam’s voicemail says to ask whoever’s on shift. That’s you, right?”

“I’m just covering. Try the website—portal’s got everything.”

“The portal 404s. Look, I’m on a deadline. Where’s the actual paper schedule?”

“Binder somewhere. I’m off in ten, so maybe come back tomorrow?”

“I can’t. Whatever you do, do NOT send me to that portal—its last “update” wiped half the data. Just point me to the binder.”

“Hi—sorry, just a quick one,” Ignacio said. “I’m trying to plug the crew’s heat-stress numbers into the standard model. Is it WBGT or HSI you guys actually use?”

She didn’t stop moving. “OSHA’s got charts for that. Try their website under ‘heat illness prevention.’ I’m on my way out.”

“I checked. Their charts round everything to county level; I need site-specific temps.” He shifted, still blocking. “Do you measure the black-globe temp yourself?”

“Nope, safety keeps the meters. You’ll have to ask them—trailer up in Morrison. Bye.”

“Morrison’s an hour north and I’m on a deadline.” Impatience flickered at the edges of his voice. “Could I at least borrow the calibration sheet or the sensor log?”

Ragna’s hand tightened on her keys. “Everything’s digital now. Password changes weekly. Sorry, not my circus.”

“There must be a spreadsheet copy somewhere—Excel, whatever. I can anonymize the names.”

“Check the shared drive. Search ‘Safety.’ Look, my ride’s already running.”

“Shared drives hate me.” He was pushing now, direct and compact. “Do you know off the top of your head what correction factor you apply for direct versus shaded readings?”

“Wish I could help, really. I’ve got to scoop my kid before late fees hit.”

He exhaled. “If it helps, I only need the equation. One line. Do NOT send me to NCDC’s ftp archive—that server crashed my laptop twice. What’s the local formula?”

Torben stood by a red toolbox, neon vest unzipped, eyelids at half-mast, cradling the last of a 7-Eleven coffee. He tracked her with one wary eye, the other on the punch-clock glowing radioactive green by the stairwell.  

“You’re Torben, right?” she began. “I need a quick rundown on how you check the waterproofing after installation.”  

“Uh, not my lane,” he said, angling toward the exit. “You’ll want Arthur—he’s the hydro rep.”  

“Arthur’s on the phone for the next hour. Five minutes tops, then I’m gone. What tests do you actually run?”  

Torben scratched his neck. “Mostly pressure checks, visual, standard stuff. Arthur signs off.”  

“Which pressure checks? ASTM D5385? How do you avoid popping the membrane?”  

“We hire the hydro firm for that. Liability says don’t touch.” He lifted his hard hat, resettled it—another glance at the clock.  

“But you’re here monitoring progress. You see the techs work. What do they tape to the walls?”  

“Couple of rigs, gauges, nothing fancy.” A truck beep-beeped somewhere topside; he raised a finger. “Look, I’ve got a delivery truck coming.”  

“Fine—crayon here if you must. Are they doing flood tests right now?”  

“Flood test is Phase Two. We’re still sealing joints.” His shoulders edged away.  

Naya kept her heels planted. “So a partial flood behind the bulkhead—yes or no? And do NOT use flood water from the sump pit—if it’s got hydrocarbons it’ll skew my samples.”

“Policy says you need clearance from the senior associate first, so…” He shrugged, shoulders telegraphing exit.

“Could be in the shared drive. Or grab the guideline book from the library—section eleven, I think.”

“That reference is ten years old. I need the current numbers. Can’t you just email me the sheet?”

“Email’s archived. Takes forever to dig out. Maybe ask Karen—she’s faster.” The copier clanged; end-of-day ghosts flitting through form-feed.

“Karen’s at depositions all afternoon.” Zara planted the drawing against her hip, paper crackling. “Do NOT send me to the old drafting manual—half those values changed.”

Valeria stepped inside, boots creaking on the plywood floor, clutching two sloshing sample bottles in one hand and a checklist curling at the edges in the other. The dissolved-oxygen meter sat on the bench like a broken promise, its probe jutting from the sponge like a knife stuck in a bar of soap. The thing wouldn’t calibrate. Again.

She spotted Magnuson behind the pelican case, crouched as if hiding. His fingers worried at a knot of rubber tubing like it was the most important job in the world.

“Morning,” Valeria said, voice pitched to sound casual. “I’m getting junk numbers on DO—can you walk me through the membrane swap real quick?”

Magnuson didn’t look up. “Manual’s in the clipboard. I’ve got a pickup across the lot in five.”

She glanced at the clipboard, dangling by its cracked plastic clamp, and tried again. “Manual says rinse with distilled water, but the probe still drifts. Any tricks?”

“Try the new kit by the cooler. Ask Rachel if the salt tablets came in.”

“Rachel’s off-site,” she said, flat. “Should I condition the membrane before or after calibration?”

“After. Or before. Depends on the firmware—gotta run.”

Valeria felt the familiar tick in her jaw. She thumbed the meter’s display. “Firmware’s 3.2. One-point or two-point air cal?”

“Two-point. Look, my ride’s idling.”

“Do NOT use the sodium sulfite zero solution—old batch crashed my last cap.”

He worried a leftover stake between thumb and forefinger like a dog with a splinter. Everyone else had gone for beer and noise; only Olwen remained, scooping scraps of switchgrass into a bucket and humming something that ended on the same tired note.

Natan cleared his throat. “The left side keeps climbing no matter how tight I pack the stakes. What am I missing?”

Olwen flicked a damp towel across the table and didn’t look up. “Did you double-check your stake lengths? Most folks trim after soaking.”

“They’re matched within a millimeter. Still lifts like it’s caffeinated.”

“Might just re-soak ’em; the difference shows up when they swell.” She angled her wrist toward the window—the Subaru’s windshield was already powdered with pine pollen.

“Been in over an hour,” Natan said. He flexed the crooked wall in demonstration. “Could the two-by-two weave be pulling diagonally?”

Olwen tugged the bucket onto her hip. “Could swap to three-by-one but then you’d lose hex strength. Your call.”

Natan sucked on a tooth. “Rivet pins with copper nails—bad idea?”

“Too stiff; basket remembers every nail once it dries.” She stepped over a coil of lashings on the floorboards, hunting the path to the steps.

“Right, so the usual soak-steam-creep,” Natan said, half to himself, “but do NOT use extra weavers on the short side. Tried that once and split the whole rim.”

Joachim knelt on the salt-stained deck, pliers dangling from his grease-smudged hand, and raised his voice above the gulls. “Hey, can you actually eyeball this wiring? The pump works, but the splice looks… generous.”

Priyanka didn’t bother looking up from her phone. “Not my hull, not my circus. Ask the yard electrician.”

Across the dock the sunset glare caught on cracked varnish. “Yard guy went home an hour ago,” Joachim said. “Just flag which crimps look sketch.”

“I’m quitting dock work after last week’s tetanus scare; find another rube.” She took a miserly sip of the coffee that had gone room-temperature twenty minutes earlier and flicked her thumb across an unchanged screen.

Joachim ducked back under the companionway and pointed. “Ten seconds. The red wire jumps to brown, then dives out of sight—normal?”

“If it’s heat-shrink and solder, sure. If butt connectors, burn it all.” She adjusted the hood as though against rain that wasn’t coming.

With the side cutters he snapped off one corroded cap. “The yard used unsealed crimp caps; should I re-do every joint?”

Priyanka finally met his eyes, shrugged. “Whole loom, yeah. Also buy real adhesive-lined heat-shrink. And beer.”

He dangled the severed wire like evidence. “Got it. Did you bring the multimeter—the one with the clamp?”

Andre poked the limp neon noodle of TPU with a hex key, as if it might confess.  
“Do cold pulls ever work with TPU, or are they a waste of time?”  

Beatriz, coat sliding off one shoulder, checked the wall clock: 9:19.  
“They mostly stretch, so yeah, mostly waste of time.”  

He nodded, fingers drumming the frame.  
“Okay, so I'll skip that. What about bumping the flow percentage to one-twenty?”  

“You could, but if it's under-extruding, check the bowden first.”  

“Bowden looks clear.” He flicked the tubing for emphasis. “Retraction settings?”  

“Dial the distance back two millimetres and slow the speed. That usually fixes it.”
